questions.title: Classify a temperature reading
questions.promptHtml: A laboratory records a temperature of −7 °C. Which statement correctly classifies the number −7?
questions.hint: An integer can be negative. A rational number can be written as a fraction of two integers.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. −7 is an integer because it has no fractional part.
  2. −7 = −7/1, so it is also rational. It is not a natural number.

options.label: Integer and rational, but not natural
Neither an integer nor a rational number

questions.title: Calculate in the correct order
questions.promptHtml:
Calculate 72 ÷ (3 × 4) + 23 − 5.

Enter a whole number.
questions.hint: Complete the brackets and the power first. Then divide, and finally add and subtract.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Inside the brackets: 3 × 4 = 12. The power is 23 = 8.
  2. 72 ÷ 12 + 8 − 5 = 6 + 8 − 5 = 9.

questions.title: Prepare a laboratory mixture
questions.promptHtml:
A laboratory mixes liquids A and B in the ratio 3 : 5. It needs 640 mL in total.

How much of each liquid is needed? Enter whole numbers in mL.
questions.hint: There are 3 + 5 equal parts. Find the volume of one part first.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total parts = 3 + 5 = 8. One part = 640 ÷ 8 = 80 mL.
  2. Liquid A: 3 × 80 = 240 mL. Liquid B: 5 × 80 = 400 mL.
  3. The volumes sum to 640 mL and the ratio 240 : 400 simplifies to 3 : 5.

questions.title: A price rises, then returns
questions.promptHtml:
A textbook price rises from ¥240 to ¥276.

Find the percentage increase. Then find the percentage discount on ¥276 that would return the price to ¥240. Give both percentages to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Percentage change = change ÷ starting value × 100. The starting value is different in the second calculation.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Price change = 276 − 240 = ¥36.
  2. Increase = (36 ÷ 240) × 100 = 15.00%.
  3. To return to ¥240, the discount uses ¥276 as its base: (36 ÷ 276) × 100 = 13.043478…%, or 13.04%.

questions.title: Model a delivery cost
questions.promptHtml:
A delivery cost is calculated using C = 18 + 2.4x, where C is the cost in yuan and x is the distance in kilometres.

Calculate C when x = 7.5. Then find x when C = 60. Give both answers to 1 decimal place.
questions.hint: Substitute x = 7.5 for the first part. For the second, subtract 18 from both sides before dividing by 2.4.

questions.title: Convert measurements
questions.promptHtml:
Convert the following measurements:

  • 2.75 km to metres.
  • 960 mL to litres.
  • 90 km/h to metres per second.

Use whole numbers for metres and m/s, and 2 decimal places for litres.
questions.hint: 1 km = 1,000 m; 1 L = 1,000 mL; 1 hour = 3,600 seconds.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 2.75 × 1,000 = 2,750 m.
  2. 960 ÷ 1,000 = 0.96 L.
  3. 90 km/h = 90,000 m ÷ 3,600 s = 25 m/s.

questions.title: Arrange six display items
questions.promptHtml:
A shop places six different products in a single row. Each product is used once.

How many different arrangements are possible? Also give the value of 0!. Enter whole numbers.
questions.hint: For six different items in a row, multiply 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1. Remember the definition of 0!.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. There are 6 choices for the first position, then 5, then 4, and so on.
  2. 6! = 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 720 arrangements.
  3. By definition, 0! = 1. There is one way to arrange an empty selection.

questions.title: Assign three different roles
questions.promptHtml:
A team has 9 members. It must appoint a supervisor, an assistant and an inspector. One person cannot hold more than one role.

How many different assignments are possible? Enter a whole number.
questions.hint: The roles are different, so order matters. There are 9 choices, then 8, then 7.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The three roles are distinct: choosing the same three people for different roles creates a different assignment.
  2. P(9, 3) = 9! ÷ (9 − 3)! = 9 × 8 × 7 = 504 assignments.

questions.title: Choose a review committee
questions.promptHtml:
A team has 9 members. It selects a committee of 3 people. All committee members have the same role.

How many different committees can be formed? Enter a whole number.
questions.hint: The order of the three people does not matter. Divide the number of ordered selections by 3!.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Order does not matter because the committee has no separate roles.
  2. C(9, 3) = 9! ÷ (3! × 6!) = (9 × 8 × 7) ÷ (3 × 2 × 1) = 84 committees.

questions.title: A terminating decimal
questions.promptHtml: Which description fits 0.375?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. 0.375 = 375/1000 = 3/8, so it is rational; it has a non-zero fractional part.

questions.title: A square root
questions.promptHtml: Which description fits √49?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. √49 = 7. It is a positive whole number and can be written as 7/1.

questions.title: An irrational length
questions.promptHtml: Which number is irrational?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. √2 cannot be written as a ratio of integers. The other three numbers can.

questions.title: A repeating decimal
questions.promptHtml: The decimal 0.272727… repeats forever. How is it classified?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. A repeating decimal is rational: 0.272727… = 27/99 = 3/11.

questions.title: A negative fraction
questions.promptHtml: Which set contains −11/4?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. −11/4 is a ratio of two integers with a non-zero denominator, but equals −2.75 rather than an integer.

questions.title: Evaluate 18 − 3 × (2 + 1)^2
questions.promptHtml: Calculate 18 − 3 × (2 + 1)2.
questions.hint: Brackets and powers come before multiplication or division; equal-priority operations go left to right.

questions.title: Evaluate (48 ÷ 6 + 2) × 1.5
questions.promptHtml: Calculate (48 ÷ 6 + 2) × 1.5.
questions.hint: Brackets and powers come before multiplication or division; equal-priority operations go left to right.

questions.title: Evaluate −4^2 + (−4)^2
questions.promptHtml: Calculate −42 + (−4)2.
questions.hint: Brackets and powers come before multiplication or division; equal-priority operations go left to right.

questions.title: Evaluate 36 ÷ 3 × 2 − 5
questions.promptHtml: Calculate 36 ÷ 3 × 2 − 5.
questions.hint: Brackets and powers come before multiplication or division; equal-priority operations go left to right.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Division and multiplication have equal priority: work left to right.
  2. 36 ÷ 3 × 2 = 12 × 2 = 24; 24 − 5 = 19.

questions.title: Evaluate 2.4 + 3 × (5.5 − 1.5) ÷ 2
questions.promptHtml: Calculate 2.4 + 3 × (5.5 − 1.5) ÷ 2.
questions.hint: Brackets and powers come before multiplication or division; equal-priority operations go left to right.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Brackets give 4.
  2. 3 × 4 ÷ 2 = 6; 2.4 + 6 = 8.4.

questions.title: Evaluate (7 + 5)! ÷ 11!
questions.promptHtml: Calculate (7 + 5)! ÷ 11!.
questions.hint: Brackets and powers come before multiplication or division; equal-priority operations go left to right.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. (7 + 5)! = 12! = 12 × 11!.
  2. Cancel 11! to obtain 12.

questions.title: Allocate a research budget
questions.promptHtml: A research budget is split between equipment and staffing in the ratio 3:7. The total is 8500. Find both shares.
questions.hint: Divide the total by the total number of ratio parts.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total parts = 10; one part = 8500 ÷ 10 = 850.
  2. First share = 2550; second share = 5950.

questions.title: Mix cleaning solution
questions.promptHtml: Concentrate and water are mixed in the ratio 2:9. The total is 825. Find both shares.
questions.hint: Divide the total by the total number of ratio parts.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total parts = 11; one part = 825 ÷ 11 = 75.
  2. First share = 150; second share = 675.

questions.title: Divide laboratory time
questions.promptHtml: Microscopy and sample preparation share the available hours in the ratio 5:3. The total is 14. Find both shares.
questions.hint: Divide the total by the total number of ratio parts.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total parts = 8; one part = 14 ÷ 8 = 1.75.
  2. First share = 8.75; second share = 5.25.

questions.title: Recover the total mixture
questions.promptHtml: A mixture has active ingredient to carrier in the ratio 2:7. It contains 175 mL of carrier. Find the active ingredient and total volume.
questions.hint: The 175 mL corresponds to seven parts, not nine.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. One part = 175/7 = 25 mL.
  2. Active ingredient = 2 × 25 = 50 mL; total = 225 mL.

questions.title: Scale a treatment batch
questions.promptHtml: A batch for 12 test samples uses 45 mL of reagent. At the same rate, how much is needed for 38 samples?
questions.hint: Find the amount per sample.

questions.title: Simplify a decimal ratio
questions.promptHtml: Simplify 1.2:0.45 to the smallest positive whole-number ratio.
questions.hint: Multiply both terms by 100, then divide by their greatest common factor.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 1.2:0.45 = 120:45.
  2. Divide both by 15 to obtain 8:3.

questions.title: More pumps, less time
questions.promptHtml: Four identical pumps empty a tank in 18 hours. How long do six such pumps take, assuming constant rates and no interference?
questions.hint: The total number of pump-hours stays constant.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 4 × 18 = 72 pump-hours.
  2. 72/6 = 12 hours.

questions.title: Clinic visits rise
questions.promptHtml: A recorded value changes from 240 to 294. Calculate the percentage change. Use a negative answer for a decrease.
questions.hint: Use the original value as the denominator.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Change = 54.
  2. Percentage change = (54/240) × 100 = 22.50%.

questions.title: Defect count falls
questions.promptHtml: A recorded value changes from 160 to 124. Calculate the percentage change. Use a negative answer for a decrease.
questions.hint: Use the original value as the denominator.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Change = -36.
  2. Percentage change = (-36/160) × 100 = -22.50%.

questions.title: Energy use changes
questions.promptHtml: A recorded value changes from 82.5 to 75.9. Calculate the percentage change. Use a negative answer for a decrease.
questions.hint: Use the original value as the denominator.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Change = -6.6.
  2. Percentage change = (-6.6/82.5) × 100 = -8.00%.

questions.title: Find the price before a discount
questions.promptHtml: After a 15% discount, equipment costs ¥714. What was its original price?
questions.hint: The sale price is 85% of the original.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 0.85 × original = 714.
  2. Original = 714/0.85 = ¥840.

questions.title: Two successive increases
questions.promptHtml: A laboratory fee of ¥500 rises by 10%, then by a further 8%. Find the final fee and the overall percentage increase.
questions.hint: Apply the second increase to the new fee.

questions.title: Recover after a fall
questions.promptHtml: Output falls from 250 units to 200 units. What percentage increase from 200 is needed to return to 250?
questions.hint: The recovery percentage uses 200 as its base.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Required increase = 50 units.
  2. 50/200 × 100 = 25%.

questions.title: Percentage points and relative change
questions.promptHtml: A response rate rises from 40% to 52%. Find the increase in percentage points and the relative percentage increase.
questions.hint: Subtract the rates for percentage points; divide that change by the original rate for relative change.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 52 − 40 = 12 percentage points.
  2. 12/40 × 100 = 30% relative increase.

questions.title: Discount followed by tax
questions.promptHtml: An item has a listed price of ¥1250. A 12% discount is applied, then 6% tax is charged on the discounted price. Find the amount paid.
questions.hint: Use one multiplier for the discount and another for the tax.

questions.title: Substitute a negative value
questions.promptHtml: Evaluate y = 3x² − 2x + 5 when x = −2.
questions.hint: Substitute carefully, or undo the operations in reverse order.

questions.title: Solve a linear equation
questions.promptHtml: Solve 4x + 7 = 31.
questions.hint: Substitute carefully, or undo the operations in reverse order.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Subtract 7: 4x = 24.
  2. Divide by 4: x = 6.

questions.title: Rearrange a cost model
questions.promptHtml: Total cost is C = 180 + 12q. Find q when C = 780.
questions.hint: Substitute carefully, or undo the operations in reverse order.

questions.title: Use a rate formula
questions.promptHtml: Speed v = d/t. A sample travels 135 metres in 18 seconds. Calculate v in metres per second.
questions.hint: Substitute carefully, or undo the operations in reverse order.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. v = 135/18.
  2. v = 7.5 metres per second.

questions.title: Solve with a bracket
questions.hint: Substitute carefully, or undo the operations in reverse order.
questions.solutionHtml:

questions.promptHtml: Calculate z = (x − μ)/σ when x = 46, μ = 52 and σ = √9.
questions.hint: Substitute carefully, or undo the operations in reverse order.

questions.promptHtml: Convert 0.085 litres to millilitres.

questions.promptHtml: Convert 750 micrograms to milligrams. Use 1000 micrograms = 1 milligram.
questions.hint: Write the conversion factor with units before calculating.

questions.promptHtml: Convert 2.35 hours to minutes.
questions.hint: Write the conversion factor with units before calculating.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. 2.35 × 60 = 141 minutes. Decimal hours are not hours and minutes.

questions.promptHtml: Convert 7.5 inches to centimetres. Use 1 inch = 2.54 cm.
questions.hint: Write the conversion factor with units before calculating.

questions.promptHtml: Convert 0.032 m² to cm². Use 1 m = 100 cm.
questions.hint: Write the conversion factor with units before calculating.

questions.hint: Write the conversion factor with units before calculating.

questions.title: Order five specimens
questions.promptHtml: Five distinct specimens are placed in a row. How many orders are possible?
questions.hint: Decide whether order or distinct roles matter. All objects or people are distinct.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Use factorial: 5!.
  2. The number of possibilities is 120.

questions.title: Order seven presentations
questions.promptHtml: Seven different presentations are scheduled in seven time slots. How many schedules are possible?
questions.hint: Decide whether order or distinct roles matter. All objects or people are distinct.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Use factorial: 7!.
  2. The number of possibilities is 5040.

questions.title: Assign two officers
questions.promptHtml: From nine staff, choose one chair and a different secretary. How many assignments are possible?
questions.hint: Decide whether order or distinct roles matter. All objects or people are distinct.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Use permutation: 9!/(7)!.
  2. The number of possibilities is 72.

questions.title: Rank three finalists
questions.promptHtml: Seven finalists compete for first, second and third place, with no ties. How many ordered results are possible?
questions.hint: Decide whether order or distinct roles matter. All objects or people are distinct.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Use permutation: 7!/(4)!.
  2. The number of possibilities is 210.

questions.title: Select three samples
questions.promptHtml: Choose three of eight distinct samples for testing. Order does not matter. How many selections are possible?
questions.hint: Decide whether order or distinct roles matter. All objects or people are distinct.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Use combination: 8!/(3! × 5!).
  2. The number of possibilities is 56.

questions.title: Select four representatives
questions.promptHtml: Choose a four-person committee from ten people, with no assigned roles. How many committees are possible?
questions.hint: Decide whether order or distinct roles matter. All objects or people are distinct.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Use combination: 10!/(4! × 6!).
  2. The number of possibilities is 210.

questions.title: Create a two-symbol label
questions.promptHtml: A label uses two different symbols chosen from six. Symbol order matters and repetition is forbidden. How many labels are possible?
questions.hint: Decide whether order or distinct roles matter. All objects or people are distinct.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Use permutation: 6!/(4)!.
  2. The number of possibilities is 30.

questions.title: Select a pair of clinics
questions.promptHtml: Choose two of nine clinics for a joint study. The clinics have equal roles. How many pairs are possible?
questions.hint: Decide whether order or distinct roles matter. All objects or people are distinct.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Use combination: 9!/(2! × 7!).
  2. The number of possibilities is 36.

questions.title: A committee with a chair
questions.promptHtml: From eight staff, select a three-person committee, then choose one of its members as chair. How many outcomes are possible?
questions.hint: Choose the committee, then its chair.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. C(8,3) = 56 committees.
  2. Each has 3 possible chairs: 56 × 3 = 168 outcomes.

questions.title: Compare repetition rules
questions.promptHtml: A three-digit laboratory code uses digits 1–5. Find the number of codes (a) with repetition allowed and (b) with no repeated digit.
questions.hint: With repetition the options stay constant; without repetition they decrease.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. With repetition: 5³ = 125.
  2. Without repetition: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60.

questions.title: Cancel factorials before calculating
questions.hint: Expand 8! only far enough to cancel 6!.

questions.title: Find the original group sizes
questions.promptHtml: The ratio of laboratory assistants to technicians is 3:5. There are 14 more technicians than assistants. Find the number in each group.
questions.hint: The difference of two ratio parts corresponds to 14 people.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 5 − 3 = 2 parts; one part = 14/2 = 7.
  2. Assistants = 3 × 7 = 21; technicians = 5 × 7 = 35.

questions.title: Recover the starting enrolment
questions.promptHtml: After increasing by 12.5%, course enrolment is 180 students. What was the enrolment before the increase?
questions.hint: 180 is 112.5% of the original enrolment.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Original × 1.125 = 180.
  2. Original = 180/1.125 = 160 students.

questions.title: Read membership and count distinct elements
questions.promptHtml:
A set is written as A = {2, 2, 4, 7, 9}. Repeating a value does not add a new element.

Choose the true membership statement and give n(A).
questions.hint: Count distinct values, then read ∈ as “is an element of”.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The distinct elements are 2, 4, 7 and 9. Therefore n(A) = 4.
  2. The statement 4 ∈ A is true because 4 appears in A.

questions.title: Find the common elements
questions.promptHtml: Let A = {1, 3, 5, 6} and B = {2, 3, 6, 8}. Select A ∩ B.
questions.hint: An intersection contains only elements that appear in both sets.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 3 and 6 occur in both A and B.
  2. Therefore A ∩ B = {3, 6}.

questions.title: Combine material options
questions.promptHtml:
A supplier offers material set A = {glass, steel, paper}. Another offers B = {paper, bamboo}.

Choose A ∪ B and give its number of elements.
questions.hint: A union includes every distinct element in either set. Count paper once.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Combine the options without repeating paper.
  2. A ∪ B = {glass, steel, paper, bamboo}, so n(A ∪ B) = 4.

questions.title: Use the universal set for a complement
questions.promptHtml:
The universal set of sample labels is U = {101, 102, 103, 104, 105, 106}. The inspected samples are I = {101, 103, 106}.

Which set is Ic, the samples in U that have not been inspected?
questions.hint: Start with U and remove every element in I.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Remove 101, 103 and 106 from U.
  2. The complement is Ic = {102, 104, 105}. Values outside U do not belong in this complement.

questions.title: Distinguish an empty set from a set containing zero
questions.promptHtml:
Let E = {2, 4, 6} and O = {1, 3, 5}.

Select E ∩ O and give n(E ∩ O).
questions.hint: No number in these lists is both even and odd. The empty set and {0} are different.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. There are no shared elements, so E ∩ O = ∅.
  2. An empty set has 0 elements. The set {0} would have one element, namely zero.

questions.title: Complete a two-group survey
questions.promptHtml:
Of 80 laboratory staff, 46 use software A, 39 use software B, and 17 use both. Each software total includes the staff who use both.

Find the numbers using A only, B only, at least one package, and neither. Enter whole numbers.
questions.hint: Place the 17 shared users first. Subtract them from each total before finding the union.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A only = 46 − 17 = 29. B only = 39 − 17 = 22.
  2. At least one = 29 + 17 + 22 = 68. Neither = 80 − 68 = 12.
  3. Check all four separate groups: 29 + 17 + 22 + 12 = 80.

questions.title: Recover a missing overlap
questions.promptHtml:
A survey of 120 students records 72 using the library (L), 65 using the study centre (S), and 18 using neither. Students can use both.

Find n(L ∪ S), n(L ∩ S), and the number using the library only.
questions.hint: First subtract neither from the total. The extra count in 72 + 65 is the overlap.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. At least one = 120 − 18 = 102.
  2. Both = 72 + 65 − 102 = 35.
  3. Library only = 72 − 35 = 37. For a check, study centre only = 65 − 35 = 30, and 37 + 35 + 30 + 18 = 120.

questions.title: Correct a double count
questions.promptHtml:
A group has 60 people. Of these, 44 speak language A, 32 speak language B and 20 speak both.

A student writes: “44 + 32 = 76, so 76 people speak at least one of the two languages.” Identify the error and give the correct number speaking at least one.
questions.hint: The 20 bilingual people appear in both totals.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Adding the totals counts every bilingual person twice.
  2. Subtract the overlap once: 44 + 32 − 20 = 56.
  3. The remaining 60 − 56 = 4 speak neither language.

options.label: People who speak both were counted twice.
People who speak both should be excluded entirely.
Every union must be divided by two.
The two language totals cannot overlap.

fields.label: Correct number speaking at least one

questions.title: Recognise a quadratic after simplifying
questions.promptHtml:
Which equation is quadratic after like terms have been simplified?

For the equation you select, give a, b and c in the form ax² + bx + c = 0.
questions.hint: Move all terms to one side. An equation is quadratic only if the resulting x² coefficient is non-zero.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. For 3x² + 2x = 7, standard form is 3x² + 2x − 7 = 0. Thus a = 3, b = 2, c = −7.
  2. In x² + 4x = x² + 9, the x² terms cancel, leaving a linear equation. The remaining options are linear and cubic.

questions.title: Solve a quadratic by factoring
questions.promptHtml: Solve x² − 7x + 12 = 0 by factoring. Enter the smaller root first and the larger root second.
questions.hint: Find two numbers whose product is 12 and whose sum is −7.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The numbers are −3 and −4, so x² − 7x + 12 = (x − 3)(x − 4).
  2. A product is zero when at least one factor is zero. The roots are 3 and 4.
  3. Check: 9 − 21 + 12 = 0 and 16 − 28 + 12 = 0.

questions.title: Find a negative and a positive root
questions.promptHtml: Solve x² + 2x − 15 = 0. Enter the smaller root first and the larger root second.
questions.hint: The two factor numbers must multiply to −15 and add to 2.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Factor: (x + 5)(x − 3) = 0.
  2. Set each bracket to zero: x + 5 = 0 or x − 3 = 0. The roots are −5 and 3.
  3. Both satisfy the original equation: 25 − 10 − 15 = 0 and 9 + 6 − 15 = 0.

questions.title: Use the quadratic formula with signed coefficients
questions.promptHtml:
Solve 2x² − x − 6 = 0 using the quadratic formula.

Give the smaller and larger roots to 1 decimal place.
questions.hint: Use a = 2, b = −1 and c = −6. Keep their signs in b² − 4ac.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The discriminant is (−1)² − 4(2)(−6) = 1 + 48 = 49.
  2. x = [1 ± √49] / 4 = (1 ± 7) / 4.
  3. The roots are −1.5 and 2.0. Check: 2(−1.5)² − (−1.5) − 6 = 0, and 2(2)² − 2 − 6 = 0.

questions.title: Round roots only at the end
questions.promptHtml: Solve x² − 4x − 1 = 0. Give both roots to 3 decimal places, smaller first.
questions.hint: The discriminant is 20. Keep the square root unrounded until the final answers.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. a = 1, b = −4 and c = −1. Therefore x = [4 ± √(16 + 4)] / 2.
  2. This simplifies to x = 2 ± √5.
  3. The roots are −0.2360679… and 4.2360679…, giving −0.236 and 4.236 to 3 d.p.

questions.title: Find the root a student missed
questions.promptHtml:
A student solves x² = 49 and writes “x = 7, because √49 = 7.”

Which correction is needed? Enter both roots, smaller first.
questions.hint: The square-root symbol means the non-negative square root, but an equation involving x² can also have a negative solution.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Both 7² and (−7)² equal 49.
  2. The principal square root √49 is 7, while the equation x² = 49 has two roots: −7 and 7.

options.label: No correction: only the positive root is allowed.

questions.title: Choose a physically possible quadratic root
questions.promptHtml:
A rectangular label has width x cm and length (x + 3) cm. Its area is 54 cm².

Find the width and length, then explain why one mathematical root must be rejected.
questions.hint: Use area = width × length. After solving, both dimensions must be positive.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. x(x + 3) = 54, so x² + 3x − 54 = 0.
  2. Factor: (x + 9)(x − 6) = 0, giving x = −9 or x = 6.
  3. A width cannot be negative, so choose width 6 cm and length 9 cm. Their area is 6 × 9 = 54 cm².

options.label: It gives a negative physical width and length.
It does not solve the quadratic equation.
Negative numbers can never solve equations.
Always choose the largest root regardless of context.

questions.title: Simplify before substituting
questions.promptHtml: Simplify 4x − 3 + 2(x + 5) − x. Then find its value when x = −2.
questions.hint: Expand the bracket first, then collect x terms and constants separately.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Expand: 4x − 3 + 2x + 10 − x.
  2. Collect like terms: (4 + 2 − 1)x + (−3 + 10) = 5x + 7.
  3. At x = −2: 5(−2) + 7 = −3.

questions.title: Solve with a variable on both sides
questions.promptHtml: Solve 4(x − 2) + 3 = 2x + 9. Then give the common value of the left and right sides when you substitute your solution.
questions.hint: Expand the bracket, collect like terms and keep both sides balanced.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Expand and simplify: 4x − 8 + 3 = 2x + 9, so 4x − 5 = 2x + 9.
  2. Subtract 2x and add 5 to both sides: 2x = 14, giving x = 7.
  3. Check the original sides: 4(7 − 2) + 3 = 23 and 2(7) + 9 = 23.

questions.title: Repair an expansion sign error
questions.promptHtml:
A student expands −2(3x − 4) as −6x − 8.

Select the correct expansion and evaluate the original expression at x = 2.
questions.hint: Multiply −2 by each term inside the bracket, keeping the sign of each term.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. −2 × 3x = −6x and −2 × (−4) = +8.
  2. The correct expansion is −6x + 8.
  3. At x = 2: −6(2) + 8 = −4. Direct check: −2(6 − 4) = −4.

questions.title: Explain equal-priority operations
questions.promptHtml:
A student writes 30 ÷ 5 × 2 = 30 ÷ 10 = 3.

Select the rule that fixes the first incorrect step, then give the correct result.
questions.hint: Multiplication and division share the same priority. Read their sequence from left to right.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The first operation is 30 ÷ 5 = 6, followed by 6 × 2 = 12.
  2. The incorrect step treats multiplication as always preceding division. At equal priority, calculate from left to right.

options.label: Always complete every multiplication before any division.
Do multiplication and division from left to right.
Do multiplication and division from right to left.
Insert brackets around 5 × 2 whenever division appears.

questions.title: Explain why distinct roles change the count
questions.promptHtml:
A team chooses a chair and a different secretary from 7 members. A student gives C(7, 2) = 21.

Explain the error and give the correct number of appointments.
questions.hint: Swapping the chair and secretary changes the outcome.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The combination counts pairs without distinguishing their roles. Each pair has two assignments.
  2. There are 7 choices of chair and 6 remaining choices of secretary: 7 × 6 = 42.
  3. Equivalently, 21 pairs × 2 role assignments = 42.

options.label: The two roles are different, so swapping people creates another outcome.
The same person must hold both roles.
Selecting a secretary replaces the chair.

questions.title: Judge a load against a stated mass limit
questions.promptHtml:
For a mathematical planning check, a load has mass 1,900 kg and a handling system has a stated mass limit of 4,200 lb. Use 1 kg ≈ 2.205 lb.

Convert the load to pounds to 1 decimal place and decide whether it meets this mass limit. This question checks only the stated mass limit.
questions.hint: Convert the load and limit to the same unit before comparing.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Load ≈ 1,900 × 2.205 = 4,189.5 lb.
  2. The load is 4,200 − 4,189.5 = 10.5 lb below the stated limit. It meets this mass criterion.
  3. Expressing the load in pounds changes the number and unit, not the physical mass.

fields.label: Comparison with the stated mass limit

options.label: Cannot compare because 1,900 is smaller than 4,200.

questions.title: Repair a percentage-change denominator
questions.promptHtml:
A price falls from ¥250 to ¥200. A student calculates the decrease as (50 ÷ 200) × 100 = 25%.

Select the denominator required for the percentage decrease and calculate the correct percentage. Enter a positive percentage for the decrease.
questions.hint: Percentage change compares the amount of change with the starting value.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The decrease is ¥250 − ¥200 = ¥50. The starting price is ¥250.
  2. Percentage decrease = (50 ÷ 250) × 100 = 20%.
  3. The student’s 25% would describe the increase from ¥200 back to ¥250, which uses a different starting price.

questions.title: Connected case: bottle features and product choices
questions.promptHtml:
A bottle design team surveys 160 students. Of these, 96 request a reusable bottle, 88 request insulation, and 24 request neither. Each feature total includes people selecting both.

The team can offer one of 4 colours, one of 3 sizes and one of 2 lid types. Every combination is available.

Find the number requesting at least one feature, the number requesting both, the percentage of all respondents requesting both, and the number of product versions. Then select the conclusion supported by the survey. Enter whole numbers.
questions.hint: Recover the overlap from the survey totals. Count versions using one choice from each independent design category.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. At least one = 160 − 24 = 136.
  2. Both = 96 + 88 − 136 = 48. The other regions are reusable only 48 and insulation only 40. Their sum with both and neither is 160.
  3. Both as a percentage of all respondents = 48 ÷ 160 × 100 = 30%.
  4. Product versions = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24. This counts available combinations, not customer demand for each version.
  5. 136 ÷ 160 × 100 = 85% of the respondents requested at least one feature. The given counts do not establish the same percentage for all students.

fields.label: Respondents requesting at least one feature
Percentage of all respondents requesting both

options.label: 85% of the 160 respondents requested at least one feature.
85% of every student at the university requests at least one feature.
Each of the 24 versions will have equal demand.
Every surveyed student will buy a bottle.

extension.promptHtml: In two sentences, explain why the survey does not prove that 85% of all university students want at least one feature. Name one piece of information about survey selection you would need.
extension.modelAnswerHtml: The 85% describes the 160 respondents. Before making a claim about all university students, we need to know how those respondents were selected and whether important groups were excluded.
rubric: Identify the 160 respondents as the group directly described.
Explain that wider generalisation needs evidence about selection.
Name a relevant check, such as who could be selected or how selection occurred.

questions.title: Connected case: production inputs and paid orders
questions.promptHtml:
A workshop plans 300 laboratory trays, each containing 720 g of accepted material. Production loses 10% of the input mass. The input mixture contains recycled and new material in the ratio 3 : 2, and the loss affects both materials proportionally.

Recycled material is sold in complete 20 kg sacks. The workshop has 200 confirmed paid orders. Each ordered tray has list price ¥45 and a 12% discount.

Calculate the total accepted mass, required input mass, recycled and new input masses, minimum number of recycled-material sacks, selling price and revenue from the confirmed orders. Use kg for masses, whole sacks, and 2 decimal places for money.
questions.hint: Convert grams to kilograms, work backwards through the 10% loss, then divide the input in the ratio 3:2. Revenue uses the confirmed orders.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Accepted mass = 300 × 720 ÷ 1,000 = 216 kg.
  2. 90% of the input survives. Required input = 216 ÷ 0.90 = 240 kg.
  3. There are 5 ratio parts. Recycled input = (3/5) × 240 = 144 kg; new input = (2/5) × 240 = 96 kg.
  4. 144 ÷ 20 = 7.2 sacks. Buy 8 complete sacks, providing 160 kg. Only 144 kg enters this batch.
  5. Selling price = 45 × 0.88 = ¥39.60. Revenue from 200 paid orders = 200 × 39.60 = ¥7,920.00.
  6. The revenue calculation covers the 200 paid orders. It does not establish that the other 100 planned trays will sell.

fields.label: Minimum whole sacks of recycled material

options.label: The 200 confirmed paid orders produce ¥7,920 of revenue under the stated pricing rule.
All 300 planned trays will sell at the same price.
Profit is ¥7,920 because revenue and profit are the same.
Every future batch will produce exactly the same revenue.

questions.title: Study student travel times
questions.promptHtml:
A university has 6,000 students. Researchers randomly select 120 students and find that their mean daily travel time is 43.5 minutes.

Identify the population, the sample and the type of numerical summary reported.
questions.hint: The population is the whole group of interest. A statistic summarises a sample; a parameter summarises the whole population.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The population is all 6,000 university students.
  2. The sample is the 120 selected students.
  3. 43.5 minutes is a statistic because it was calculated from the sample. The mean for all 6,000 students would be a population parameter.

questions.title: Classify factory variables
questions.promptHtml:
A factory records each employee’s department, the number of defective items in a batch, and the mass of an item in grams.

Classify each variable. Treat mass as a measurement, even if the instrument rounds its display.
questions.hint: Categories name groups. Counts are usually discrete; measurements are usually continuous.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Department is qualitative: it describes a category, such as Sales or Production.
  2. Number of defective items is quantitative and discrete: the count takes whole-number values.
  3. Mass is quantitative and continuous: in principle it can take any value within a measurement range.

questions.title: Match four sampling plans
questions.promptHtml:
Identify the method used in each plan:

  1. A computer randomly selects 60 different IDs from the full student list.
  2. After a random start, a researcher selects every 20th student on a list.
  3. A researcher randomly selects 20 students from each year group.
  4. A researcher randomly selects three classes and surveys every student in those classes.
questions.hint: Stratified sampling takes some people from every group. Cluster sampling takes everyone from selected groups.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Plan 1 uses simple random sampling: the IDs are selected randomly from the complete list.
  2. Plan 2 uses systematic sampling: it follows a fixed interval after a random start.
  3. Plan 3 uses stratified sampling: each year group contributes a random sample.
  4. Plan 4 uses cluster sampling: whole selected classes are surveyed.

questions.title: Select records systematically
questions.promptHtml:
A clinic has a list of 1,000 patient records, numbered 1 to 1,000. It needs a systematic sample of 50 records.

The random starting record is 13. Find the sampling interval, the second selected record and the final selected record. Enter whole numbers.
questions.hint: Use k = N ÷ n. The selected records are 13, 13 + k, 13 + 2k, and so on.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Sampling interval: k = 1,000 ÷ 50 = 20.
  2. The second selected record is 13 + 20 = 33.
  3. The 50th and final selected record is 13 + 49(20) = 993.

questions.title: Review a satisfaction survey
questions.promptHtml:
A university posts a survey link on its website. Students decide for themselves whether to respond. The university uses the replies to estimate satisfaction among all students.

Identify the main sampling problem and choose the best improvement.
questions.hint: Think about whether students who feel strongly might be more likely to respond.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The survey is vulnerable to voluntary response bias: students who choose to reply may differ from other students.
  2. A better starting design is to randomly select students from the complete student list and follow up with selected nonrespondents.
  3. A larger self-selected sample alone does not remove this bias. Random selection and follow-up improve coverage, although nonresponse can still require attention.

options.label: No possible bias because everyone can access the link
The population mean is too large
Keep the link open longer and assume the bias disappears
Randomly select students from the full list and follow up with nonrespondents
Collect more volunteer responses and ignore who responds

questions.solutionHtml:
1. Ideal allocations: 125/700 × 53 = 9.4643; 215/700 × 53 = 16.2786; 360/700 × 53 = 27.2571.
  2. Rounding down gives 9 + 16 + 27 = 52. The largest remainder is 0.4643, so the first department receives the final place.
  3. Allocate 10, 16 and 27. Randomly select those numbers of distinct IDs from the complete department lists.

options.label: Select the required number of distinct IDs randomly from its complete list
Take the first names on the list
Accept volunteers until the allocation is filled
Ask the manager to nominate their preferred employees

questions.title: Equal group samples from unequal groups
questions.promptHtml:
A college has 300 Business students and 900 Engineering students. A researcher randomly selects 30 from each programme.

Identify the design and calculate each student’s selection chance as a percentage.
questions.hint: Stratified means random selection within every group. Proportional means preserving the population shares.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The design is stratified but not proportional.
  2. Business selection chance = 30/300 × 100 = 10%.
  3. Engineering selection chance = 30/900 × 100 = 3.33%.
  4. Business students have three times the selection chance. Equal sample counts from unequal populations are not proportional.

options.label: Simple random sampling of 60 from the college

questions.title: Invited, replied and supported
questions.promptHtml:
A clinic randomly invites 280 patients to a survey. 175 reply, and 119 of the respondents support Saturday appointments.

Calculate the response rate and the support percentage among respondents. Give percentages to two decimal places.
questions.hint: Response rate uses invitations as the denominator. Support among respondents uses replies.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Response rate = 175/280 × 100 = 62.50%.
  2. Support among respondents = 119/175 × 100 = 68.00%.
  3. The 105 missing replies mean that 68% does not establish support among all invitees or all patients.

questions.title: Repair the denominator in a report
questions.promptHtml:
A report says: “We invited 360 residents, received 216 replies, and counted 135 supporters. Therefore, 37.5% of respondents support the plan.”

Correct the support percentage among respondents and identify what the reported 37.5% actually measures.
questions.hint: The numerator 135 is correct. Decide which group the denominator describes.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Respondent support = 135/216 × 100 = 62.50%.
  2. 135/360 × 100 = 37.5% is the percentage of all invitees who are known supporters.
  3. It is not the support rate among respondents, and it does not establish total support among all invitees because missing views are unknown.

options.label: The exact percentage supporting across the whole city
Known supporters as a percentage of all invitees

questions.title: Could missing replies change a majority?
questions.promptHtml:
Of 240 invited students, 150 reply. Exactly 96 respondents support a proposal. All other respondents do not support it. No views are known for the nonrespondents.

Find the lowest and highest possible support percentages among the 240 invitees. Does this evidence establish support from more than half of the invitees?
questions.hint: There are 90 missing replies. For the lower bound none support; for the upper bound all support. Both bounds use 240.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Missing replies = 240 − 150 = 90.
  2. Minimum = 96/240 × 100 = 40%.
  3. Maximum = (96 + 90)/240 × 100 = 77.5%.
  4. A majority is not established: the possible range crosses 50%. These bounds concern the invitees only.

fields.label: Is a majority among invitees established?

options.label: Yes: every missing reply must support
No: possible support lies both below and above 50%

questions.title: A majority that missing replies cannot remove
questions.promptHtml:
A researcher invites 200 members of a club. 160 reply, including 112 supporters. The other 48 respondents do not support the plan.

Find the minimum and maximum possible support percentages among all invitees. Decide what can be concluded before the other 40 members reply.
questions.hint: Compare the number of confirmed supporters with half of all invitees.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Minimum support = 112/200 × 100 = 56%.
  2. Maximum support = (112 + 40)/200 × 100 = 76%.
  3. A majority of the 200 invitees is established because confirmed supporters already exceed 100. This alone makes no claim about any wider population.

options.label: A majority cannot ever be established unless everyone replies
At least 56% of every club in the city supports
More than half of the 200 invitees support, even if all missing replies oppose

questions.title: Consistent estimates can still miss the truth
questions.promptHtml:
A simulation has a known population percentage of 50%. Repeated samples from three procedures produce these percentages:

  • A: 59, 60, 61
  • B: 40, 50, 60
  • C: 49, 50, 51

Judge precision from the spread and accuracy here from closeness to the known value.
questions.hint: A and C have the same narrow spread. Only one also stays close to 50%.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A and C are equally precise here: each has a range of 2 percentage points. B has a range of 20.
  2. C combines narrow spread with a centre at 50%.
  3. A is consistent but centred 10 percentage points too high. Consistency alone does not guarantee accuracy.

fields.label: Most precise procedures in this illustration
Procedure that is precise and centred on the truth

questions.title: More decimal places in a weak survey
questions.promptHtml:
An open website poll reports 72.438% support for a town policy. The analyst says: “Three decimal places prove that our estimate is accurate.”

Choose the best response.
questions.hint: The number of printed digits does not tell us who participated or who was missing.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The claim confuses numerical reporting detail with evidence about accuracy.
  2. Self-selection and coverage can still distort an open poll. More digits do not repair those problems.
  3. We need the selection process, target population and response information before assessing the wider claim.

options.label: Extra decimal places do not establish accurate sampling or remove bias
Three decimals guarantee accuracy within 0.001 percentage points
Rounding to a whole number would automatically remove bias

questions.title: Compare sampling costs and limitations
questions.promptHtml:
A college has 60 centres with 30 trainees each. Both plans select 180 trainees, and everyone takes part.

  • Plan A: simple random selection of individual IDs. This draw covers 45 centres.
  • Plan B: randomly select six whole centres and include all 30 trainees at each.

Fieldwork costs ¥80 per centre visited plus ¥12 per trainee. Calculate each cost and identify Plan B’s main statistical limitation.
questions.hint: Total cost = centres × 80 + trainees × 12. Consider similarity among trainees at the same centre.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A costs 45 × 80 + 180 × 12 = ¥5,760.
  2. B costs 6 × 80 + 180 × 12 = ¥2,640.
  3. B uses cluster sampling. Similar trainees in a few centres can lead to greater variation between samples. Random clusters are not automatically biased.

options.label: Plan B surveys every trainee in the college
Equal sample sizes force identical precision
Similar trainees within only six centres may reduce precision
Cluster sampling is always biased even with random selection

questions.title: Follow up the selected nonrespondents
questions.promptHtml:
A researcher randomly selects 180 patients. Only 108 reply. To fill the gap, an assistant suggests recruiting 72 volunteers from a social-media page.

Choose the best next step for the original random-sample survey.
questions.hint: The original selection process chose particular people. New volunteers do not provide those missing people’s answers.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Follow up the 72 originally selected nonrespondents using reminders and accessible response methods.
  2. Volunteers enter through a different process, so replacing missing respondents with volunteers does not preserve the original design.
  3. Follow-up helps, but it does not guarantee that all remaining nonresponse bias disappears.

options.label: Recruit any 72 volunteers and call the sample unchanged
Delete 72 existing replies so every count matches
Assume every nonrespondent has the same view as the respondents
Contact the 72 originally selected nonrespondents and offer accessible ways to reply

questions.title: Repair a measurement problem
questions.promptHtml:
A laboratory balance records every specimen as 0.24 g too heavy. The team proposes measuring twice as many specimens to solve the problem.

Choose the repair that addresses the cause.
questions.hint: Collecting more observations does not remove an error built into every measurement.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Check the balance against suitable reference masses, correct its calibration and verify it before further measurements.
  2. Doubling the sample preserves the +0.24 g shift in each new reading.
  3. Existing records need an appropriate correction or remeasurement after confirming the nature of the fault.

options.label: Round every faulty reading to more decimal places
Check and calibrate the balance against reference masses, then verify it
Double the sample while using the same faulty balance
Randomly choose a different list of specimen IDs

questions.title: Ask about the actual proposal
questions.promptHtml:
A canteen proposes adding a smaller meal option while keeping its usual portion. An initial question asks, “Don’t you agree we should remove wasteful large meals?”

Choose the best replacement question and response options.
questions.hint: A neutral question must describe adding a choice accurately, without praising or criticising it.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The replacement should ask about adding a smaller option while keeping the usual portion.
  2. Support / Oppose / Unsure permits balanced responses.
  3. The original wording both leads respondents and changes the proposal from adding an option to removing one.

options.label: Why do you oppose our excellent smaller option?
Do you agree smaller portions are better and healthier? Agree / Strongly agree
Would you support adding a smaller meal option alongside the usual portion? Support / Oppose / Unsure
Would you support replacing all usual portions with small meals? Yes / No

questions.title: An estimate is not a confirmed count
questions.promptHtml:
A simple random sample of 160 students is drawn from 3,200 students. All respond, and 58 use the university shuttle.

Use the sample proportion to estimate the number of shuttle users in the college. Then choose how to describe that result.
questions.hint: Multiply 58/160 by 3,200. Sampling does not inspect every person in the population.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Estimated count = 58/160 × 3,200 = 1,160.
  2. This is a sample-based estimate, not an established exact count.
  3. Another valid random sample could give a different estimate.

options.label: An estimate of the population count from a sample
The exact count proved by a census
The size of the selected sample
A guarantee that any other random sample gives the same result

questions.title: A comparison does not establish a cause
questions.promptHtml:
A canteen records 12 kg of leftovers on Monday using usual portions and 9 kg on Tuesday using smaller portions. The number of meals served is equal, but menus and customers differ between the days.

Calculate the percentage decrease in recorded leftovers, then choose the conclusion supported by this comparison.
questions.hint: Use Monday as the original amount. A numerical change alone cannot isolate which difference caused it.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Decrease = (12 − 9)/12 × 100 = 25%.
  2. The study recorded 25% less waste on Tuesday.
  3. It cannot attribute that decrease solely to smaller portions because the menu and customers also changed.

options.label: Recorded leftovers were 25% lower, but this comparison alone does not establish that smaller portions caused the reduction
Smaller portions are proved to reduce waste by exactly 25%
The data show no numerical change at all
Randomly counting leftovers would remove all day-to-day differences

questions.title: An imbalanced draw and a biased procedure
questions.promptHtml:
A college is 40% Engineering students. Researchers randomly select four whole classes using an equal-chance generator. In this particular draw, only 20% of selected students study Engineering.

What does this outcome establish?
questions.hint: Judge the actual sample composition separately from whether the process systematically favours a group.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Engineering is underrepresented in this draw.
  2. One imbalanced random draw does not prove that the procedure systematically favours other programmes.
  3. If both programme groups must be represented in chosen numbers, stratified selection is a suitable design for a future study.

options.label: The sample is imbalanced, but this one draw does not prove a systematically biased selection procedure
The random generator must be faulty
Every random sample must match all population percentages exactly
Cluster sampling always creates selection bias

questions.title: Library survey: from allocation to replies
questions.promptHtml:
A college has 900 Business and 600 Engineering students. It proportionally allocates 150 invitations and randomly selects distinct students within each programme.

There are 72 Business replies and 24 Engineering replies. Among all replies, 60 support longer library hours.

Find the invitation allocations, Engineering’s response rate, support among all respondents, and the most appropriate next step.
questions.hint: Keep the denominator tied to the group: allocations use 1,500; Engineering response uses Engineering invitations; overall respondent support uses 96 replies.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Business invitations = 900/1,500 × 150 = 90. Engineering invitations = 60.
  2. Engineering response rate = 24/60 × 100 = 40%.
  3. Total replies = 72 + 24 = 96. Respondent support = 60/96 × 100 = 62.50%.
  4. Follow up originally selected nonrespondents, prioritising Engineering’s lower response rate. Different response rates raise concern but do not themselves establish opinion bias.

options.label: Follow up selected nonrespondents, prioritising Engineering, with accessible ways to reply
Replace missing Engineering replies with Business volunteers
Declare that proportional invitations guarantee proportional responses
Report 62.5% as the exact college-wide support

extension.promptHtml: Optional: write two sentences describing the result and its limitation.
extension.modelAnswerHtml: Among the 96 respondents, 62.5% supported longer library hours. Engineering’s response rate was 40%, so we should follow up originally selected nonrespondents and investigate whether missing students have different views before making a college-wide claim.
rubric: State 62.5% with respondents as the reference group.
Identify the lower Engineering response rate without claiming that it proves bias.
Recommend follow-up of originally selected nonrespondents.

questions.title: Canteen survey: audit the headline
questions.promptHtml:
A college has 2,400 students. A survey invites 200 environmental-club members. 120 reply, and 84 support adding a smaller meal option.

The canteen headline reads: “70% of college students want smaller portions.” The actual proposal would keep the usual portion available.

Calculate the response rate, support among respondents, and the lowest possible support among all invitees. Then choose a defensible headline and one design repair.
questions.hint: Different percentages describe different groups. A club-only frame cannot establish a college-wide result.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Response rate = 120/200 × 100 = 60%.
  2. Respondent support = 84/120 × 100 = 70%.
  3. Minimum among invitees = 84/200 × 100 = 42% if none of the missing 80 supports.
  4. A defensible headline says: 70% of the 120 club respondents supported adding a smaller option.
  5. Use complete college lists with appropriate random selection and follow-up. More replies from only the club would not fix the original coverage problem.

options.label: 70% of all invitees certainly support the option
The survey proves smaller portions reduce food waste
70% of the 120 club respondents supported adding a smaller portion option
70% of all 2,400 students support smaller portions

fields.label: Best design repair for a college-wide opinion survey

options.label: Remove respondents who oppose smaller portions
Sample randomly from complete college lists and follow up selected nonrespondents

extension.promptHtml: Optional: write a brief corrected report about support. State one further type of evidence needed to assess whether smaller portions reduce waste.
extension.modelAnswerHtml: Among 120 environmental-club respondents, 70% supported adding a smaller option, but college-wide support remains unknown. A college-wide random survey with follow-up is needed. The waste claim requires actual leftover measurements under suitably comparable conditions; opinions about the option do not measure waste.
rubric: Limit the 70% figure to the 120 club respondents.
Identify club-only coverage or nonresponse as a limitation.
Keep opinion evidence separate from measurements of food waste.

questions.title: The research population changes
questions.promptHtml:
A researcher surveys every one of the 80 nurses in Hospital A. Their mean travel time is 32 minutes.

First the research concerns Hospital A’s nurses only. Later the same result is used to discuss all nurses employed by the city’s eight hospitals. Classify the same mean in each research question.
questions.hint: The data do not change. The target population does.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. For Hospital A’s nurses, 32 minutes is a parameter, because all members of that population were measured.
  2. For nurses across all eight hospitals, the same 32 minutes is a statistic from only part of the wider population.
  3. A complete survey of one hospital does not establish the city-wide mean.

questions.title: What a low response rate can establish
questions.promptHtml:
A simple random sample receives 300 invitations, and 60 people reply. No further information about nonrespondents is available.

A student writes: “The 20% response rate proves the estimated satisfaction level is biased downward.” Choose the best correction.
questions.hint: A low response rate raises a question about missing people. It does not reveal their opinions or the direction of any bias.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The response rate is correctly calculated: 60/300 × 100 = 20%.
  2. Low response raises concern, but bias depends on whether responding relates to satisfaction.
  3. The information does not establish that bias exists or predict its direction. Investigate and follow up missing respondents.

options.label: Low response raises concern, but neither bias nor its direction is established without relevant information about nonrespondents
Any response rate below 50% proves downward bias
Random invitation guarantees no nonresponse bias
A 20% response rate means exactly 80% are dissatisfied

questions.title: What is missing behind the percentage?
questions.promptHtml:
A university headline says: “81% support weekend teaching.” No other details appear.

Which information is most useful for assessing whether this supports a claim about all university students?
questions.hint: Look for who was eligible, how they were chosen, who replied, and what they were asked.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. We need the target population, selection method, invitation and response counts, and exact question with response options.
  2. These help assess coverage, nonresponse and wording.
  3. The percentage alone cannot establish a representative or accurate population estimate.

options.label: Only the number of decimal places in 81%
Only confirmation that the percentages add to 100%
Target population, selection procedure, invitation/reply counts, and exact wording/options
The chart colour and the report font

questions.title: Summarise daily service requests
questions.promptHtml:
A help desk receives the following numbers of service requests over six days:

12, 14, 14, 15, 17, 18

Find the mean, median and mode. Give the mean and median to 1 decimal place; give the mode as a whole number.
questions.hint: The data are already ordered. With six values, the median is the average of the third and fourth values.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total = 12 + 14 + 14 + 15 + 17 + 18 = 90. Mean = 90 ÷ 6 = 15.0 requests.
  2. Median = (14 + 15) ÷ 2 = 14.5 requests.
  3. 14 occurs twice, more often than any other value, so the mode is 14 requests.

questions.title: Reduce the effect of extreme waiting times
questions.promptHtml:
Ten waiting times, in minutes, are:

8, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 20, 44

Calculate the trimmed mean after removing 20% of the observations from each end. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
questions.hint: 20% of 10 is 2. Remove the two smallest and the two largest observations, then average what remains.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Remove 8 and 11 from the lower end, and 20 and 44 from the upper end.
  2. The remaining six values are 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 and 17. Their sum is 87.
  3. Trimmed mean = 87 ÷ 6 = 14.5 minutes. This reduces the influence of the extreme 44-minute wait.

questions.title: Describe the spread of delivery times
questions.promptHtml:
Eight delivery times, in minutes, are already ordered:

10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 24, 28, 34

Use the n + 1 method: Q1 is at position 0.25(n + 1), and Q3 at position 0.75(n + 1). Interpolate between neighbouring values.

Find the range, Q1, Q3 and IQR. Give all answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: For n = 8, the quartile positions are 2.25 and 6.75. A fractional position tells you how far to move between two values.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Range = 34 − 10 = 24.00 minutes.
  2. Q1 position = 0.25(8 + 1) = 2.25. Q1 = 12 + 0.25(15 − 12) = 12.75 minutes.
  3. Q3 position = 0.75(8 + 1) = 6.75. Q3 = 24 + 0.75(28 − 24) = 27.00 minutes.
  4. IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 27 − 12.75 = 14.25 minutes. This describes the spread of the middle 50% of the observations.

questions.title: Find a waiting-time percentile
questions.promptHtml:
Nine waiting times, in minutes, are:

5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 14, 17, 19, 24

Find the 65th percentile using position (65/100)(n + 1), with linear interpolation. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
questions.hint: The percentile position is 6.5. Find the value halfway between the sixth and seventh observations.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Position = 0.65(9 + 1) = 6.5.
  2. The sixth value is 14 and the seventh is 17.
  3. P65 = 14 + 0.5(17 − 14) = 15.5 minutes using the specified percentile convention.

questions.title: Measure variation across all batches
questions.promptHtml:
A factory produced exactly four batches today. Their defect counts were:

4, 6, 8, 10

Treat these four batches as the entire population for today. Calculate the population variance σ² and population standard deviation σ. Give both to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Find the mean, square each deviation from it, and divide the sum of squared deviations by N = 4.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Population mean μ = (4 + 6 + 8 + 10) ÷ 4 = 7.
  2. Squared deviations: (4 − 7)² + (6 − 7)² + (8 − 7)² + (10 − 7)² = 9 + 1 + 1 + 9 = 20.
  3. Population variance σ² = 20 ÷ 4 = 5.00 defects².
  4. Population standard deviation σ = √5 = 2.236067… = 2.24 defects. Standard deviation is expressed in the original units.

questions.title: Estimate variation in battery life
questions.promptHtml:
A random sample of five batteries has operating times, in hours, of:

8, 10, 12, 14, 16

Calculate the sample variance s² and sample standard deviation s. Give both to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: These batteries are a sample. Divide the sum of squared deviations by n − 1, not by n.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Sample mean x̄ = (8 + 10 + 12 + 14 + 16) ÷ 5 = 12 hours.
  2. Sum of squared deviations = (−4)² + (−2)² + 0² + 2² + 4² = 16 + 4 + 0 + 4 + 16 = 40.
  3. Sample variance s² = 40 ÷ (5 − 1) = 10.00 hours².
  4. Sample standard deviation s = √10 = 3.162277… = 3.16 hours. The n − 1 denominator is used because we are estimating population variance from a sample.

questions.title: Compare relative consistency
questions.promptHtml:
Two production lines have the following daily output summaries:

Daily output in units
LineMeanStandard deviation
A504
B808

Calculate CV = (standard deviation ÷ mean) × 100 for each line. Give percentages to 1 decimal place, then identify the line with less variation relative to its mean.
questions.hint: Compare the coefficients of variation, not just the standard deviations. The smaller CV means less relative variation.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Line A: CV = (4 ÷ 50) × 100 = 8.0%.
  2. Line B: CV = (8 ÷ 80) × 100 = 10.0%.
  3. Line A is more consistent relative to its mean because its CV is smaller.

questions.title: Recognise a long tail
questions.promptHtml:
Seven customer service times, in minutes, are:

8, 9, 10, 10, 11, 12, 40

Which direction of skewness does this pattern suggest, and which statement about the mean and median is correct?
questions.hint: The unusually large value pulls the mean towards the high end, but it has little effect on the middle observation.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Most observations lie between 8 and 12, while 40 creates a long tail to the right: the data suggest positive (right) skewness.
  2. The median is the fourth value, 10 minutes. The mean is 100 ÷ 7 = 14.2857… minutes.
  3. Therefore, the mean is greater than the median for this dataset.

questions.title: Interpret a kurtosis measure
questions.promptHtml:
A report gives a distribution’s Pearson kurtosis as 5.4. Under this convention, a normal distribution has kurtosis 3.

Calculate excess kurtosis to 1 decimal place and choose the appropriate description.
questions.hint: Excess kurtosis = Pearson kurtosis − 3. Positive excess kurtosis is described as leptokurtic.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Excess kurtosis = 5.4 − 3 = 2.4.
  2. It is positive, so the distribution is called leptokurtic relative to the normal benchmark.
  3. Kurtosis describes the influence of extreme deviations from the mean; it should not be interpreted simply as the height of the central peak.

fields.label: Description relative to the normal benchmark

questions.title: Read a box plot
questions.promptHtml:
The box plot shows delivery times. The labelled values are in minutes.

Read the median, calculate the upper outlier fence Q3 + 1.5 × IQR, and decide whether 47 minutes is an outlier by this rule. Enter whole numbers.
questions.hint: The line inside the box is the median. The box extends from Q₁ = 14 to Q₃ = 26.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The central line gives a median of 20 minutes.
  2. IQR = 26 − 14 = 12 minutes. Upper fence = 26 + 1.5(12) = 44 minutes.
  3. 47 is greater than 44, so 47 minutes is an upper outlier. The whisker ends at 38, the largest observed value that is not an outlier.

questions.title: Summarise measurement set 1
questions.promptHtml: A clinic records these waiting times in minutes: 4, 6, 6, 9, 10. Find the mean and median.
questions.hint: For the mean, divide the sum by the count. For the median, sort and find the middle.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Sum = 35; n = 5; mean = 35/5 = 7.00.
  2. The ordered data are 4, 6, 6, 9, 10; median = 6.

questions.title: Summarise measurement set 2
questions.promptHtml: A clinic records these waiting times in minutes: 12, 14, 16, 18. Find the mean and median.
questions.hint: For the mean, divide the sum by the count. For the median, sort and find the middle.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Sum = 60; n = 4; mean = 60/4 = 15.00.
  2. The ordered data are 12, 14, 16, 18; median = 15.

questions.title: Summarise measurement set 3
questions.promptHtml: A clinic records these waiting times in minutes: 2, 3, 3, 4, 8, 10. Find the mean and median.
questions.hint: For the mean, divide the sum by the count. For the median, sort and find the middle.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Sum = 30; n = 6; mean = 30/6 = 5.00.
  2. The ordered data are 2, 3, 3, 4, 8, 10; median = 3.5.

questions.title: Summarise measurement set 4
questions.promptHtml: A clinic records these waiting times in minutes: 7, 8, 8, 8, 9, 14. Find the mean and median.
questions.hint: For the mean, divide the sum by the count. For the median, sort and find the middle.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Sum = 54; n = 6; mean = 54/6 = 9.00.
  2. The ordered data are 7, 8, 8, 8, 9, 14; median = 8.

questions.title: Two equally common results
questions.promptHtml: Data: 2, 2, 4, 4, 7. What is the mode?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Both 2 and 4 occur twice, more often than 7.

questions.title: No repeated values
questions.promptHtml: Data: 3, 5, 8, 11. What is the mode?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Under the usual introductory convention, no mode is reported when every value occurs once.

questions.title: Find a modal category
questions.promptHtml: Data: bus, walk, bus, rail, bus, walk. What is the mode?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Bus appears three times, more than any other category.

options.value: Cannot have a mode for categories
options.label: Cannot have a mode for categories

questions.title: A common defect count
questions.promptHtml: Data: 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 5. What is the mode?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. The value 1 occurs three times; a mode is a most frequent value, not an average.

questions.title: Update a mean after one observation (1)
questions.promptHtml: 8 observations have mean 18. One more observation, 26, is added. Find the new mean.
questions.hint: Recover the old total before adding the new observation.

questions.title: Update a mean after one observation (2)
questions.promptHtml: 5 observations have mean 42. One more observation, 30, is added. Find the new mean.
questions.hint: Recover the old total before adding the new observation.

questions.title: Update a mean after one observation (3)
questions.promptHtml: 6 observations have mean 6.5. One more observation, 10, is added. Find the new mean.
questions.hint: Recover the old total before adding the new observation.

questions.title: Update a mean after one observation (4)
questions.promptHtml: 9 observations have mean 25. One more observation, 15, is added. Find the new mean.
questions.hint: Recover the old total before adding the new observation.

questions.title: Trim extreme readings (1)
questions.promptHtml: Readings: 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 37. Remove exactly the 1 smallest and 1 largest observation(s). Find the mean of the remaining values.
questions.hint: Sort first; remove the specified number from each end.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Remaining values: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12.
  2. Trimmed mean = 61/8 = 7.625, which rounds to 7.63 to 2 decimal places.

questions.title: Trim extreme readings (2)
questions.promptHtml: Readings: 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 20, 40. Remove exactly the 2 smallest and 2 largest observation(s). Find the mean of the remaining values.
questions.hint: Sort first; remove the specified number from each end.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Remaining values: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9.
  2. Trimmed mean = 39/6 = 6.50.

questions.title: Trim extreme readings (3)
questions.promptHtml: Readings: 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, 16, 35. Remove exactly the 1 smallest and 1 largest observation(s). Find the mean of the remaining values.
questions.hint: Sort first; remove the specified number from each end.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Remaining values: 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, 16.

questions.title: Trim extreme readings (4)

questions.title: Quartiles using the n + 1 rule (1)

questions.title: The same records, two different targets
questions.promptHtml:
A clinic records the waiting times of all 12 patients in one morning. The sum of squared deviations from their mean is 132 min².

First describe only those 12 patients. Then use these records as a sample to estimate variation among all patients this month. Select the variance divisor for each purpose. Assume the sampling limitations are considered separately.
questions.hint: Ask which group the question is trying to describe. The number of records alone does not decide the method.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. For the 12 patients in that morning, the complete target group is observed: divide by N = 12.
  2. For the larger monthly population, the 12 records form a sample: divide by n − 1 = 11.
  3. The second calculation does not make one morning representative of the whole month; that is a separate design question.

questions.title: What is missing from the SD question?
questions.promptHtml:
A question says only: “Find the standard deviation of 4, 6, 8, 10.” It does not state whether these values are the entire target population or a sample from a larger group.

What is the best response before choosing a formula?
questions.hint: A short list of numbers can describe a whole small population or a sample of a larger one.
questions.solutionHtml: Ask which target group is intended, or explicitly state the convention you are using. The population SD is √5 ≈ 2.24, whereas the sample SD is √(20/3) ≈ 2.58. Neither formula is implied merely by having four numbers.

questions.title: Repair the sample variance denominator
questions.promptHtml:
Five randomly selected batteries are used to estimate variation in a larger production run. Their sum of squared deviations is 40 hours². A student divides by 5 and reports variance 8 hours².

Find the correct sample variance and sample SD, to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: For sample variance, the divisor is one less than the sample size.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The five batteries are a sample from the production run, so use 5 − 1 = 4.
  2. s² = 40/4 = 10.00 hours².
  3. s = √10 = 3.16 hours. Dividing by 5 would describe the variance of these five observed values as a complete population.

questions.title: Zero total deviation is not zero variation
questions.promptHtml:

Find the sum of squared deviations, then correct the conclusion.
questions.hint: Opposite signed deviations cancel. Squaring stops positive and negative deviations cancelling.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Squared deviations are 4, 0 and 4, giving a total of 8 min².
  2. The observations differ, so there is variation. A zero sum of signed deviations from the mean does not imply zero SD.
