The signed deviations cancel, but the data still vary
The SD is negative because a deviation is negative

questions.title: Do not subtract the mean twice
questions.promptHtml:
For the complete population of five customers, the mean wait is 10 minutes and Σ(x − μ)² = 32 min². A student writes population variance = (32 − 10)/5.

Correct the calculation and find the population SD. Give both to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The supplied squared-deviation total already contains the subtraction of the mean from each observation.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Do not subtract 10 again: 32 is already the sum of squared deviations.
  2. σ² = 32/5 = 6.40 min².
  3. σ = √6.4 = 2.53 minutes.

questions.title: What does an SD of three minutes mean?
questions.promptHtml:
A ward has mean waiting time 12 minutes and SD 3 minutes. A manager says: “Every patient waited exactly 9 or 15 minutes.”

Which correction is justified by the two summary values?
questions.hint: SD summarises spread across a dataset. It is not the deviation of every individual observation.
questions.solutionHtml: The mean and SD describe the average and overall spread; they do not fix every individual wait. Individual deviations can differ, and SD alone does not guarantee that all waits lie between 9 and 15 minutes.

options.label: SD summarises spread; individual waits can be different distances from 12
Every wait is guaranteed to lie between 9 and 15
Some patients must have waited −3 minutes

questions.title: Classify three kurtosis reports
questions.promptHtml:
Three distributions have ordinary (Pearson) kurtosis values A = 1.8, B = 3.0 and C = 5.6. The normal reference is 3.

Classify each supplied value. You do not need to calculate kurtosis from data.
questions.hint: Compare each value with 3: below, equal to or above the normal reference.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A: 1.8 < 3, so platykurtic.
  2. B: 3.0 = 3, so mesokurtic.
  3. C: 5.6 > 3, so leptokurtic.
  4. These comparisons concern the influence of extreme deviations relative to spread; peak height alone is insufficient.

questions.title: Equal SDs can hide different shapes
questions.promptHtml:
Two complete populations of eight recorded values are:

A: 8, 8, 8, 8, 12, 12, 12, 12
B: 6, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 14

Each population has mean 10. Calculate each population SD, then judge the claim: “Equal means and SDs imply identical distribution shapes.”
questions.hint: For each set, square the deviations from 10, add them and divide by 8. Then compare where the observations occur.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A has eight squared deviations of 4: total 32. σ = √(32/8) = 2.00.
  2. B has squared deviations 16, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 16: total 32. Its σ is also 2.00.
  3. The claim is false: A has two groups away from the mean; B has six observations at the mean plus two farther extremes. Equal SDs do not determine the full shape.

options.label: True: equal SDs force the same shape
False: the locations of the observations differ despite equal SDs

questions.title: Choose typical wait and central spread
questions.promptHtml:
Most outpatient waits are between 5 and 15 minutes, but a few are over 90 minutes. You need to report a typical patient’s wait and the spread of the middle half of the waits.

Which pair is most suitable?
questions.hint: Choose a resistant measure of centre and a measure that specifically describes the middle 50%.
questions.solutionHtml: Median and IQR match both purposes. The median is less influenced by the few very long waits, and IQR measures the spread from Q₁ to Q₃. The long right tail suggests positive skewness.

questions.title: Quartile position is not the measured value
questions.promptHtml:
There are 14 ordered measurements. The 3rd is 8 cm and the 4th is 12 cm. Using the n + 1 method, a student reports “Q₁ = 3.75 cm.”

Give the correct Q₁ position and Q₁ value.
questions.hint: The position tells you where to look. Position 3.75 is three-quarters of the way from the third value to the fourth.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Q₁ position = (14 + 1)/4 = 3.75; a position has no centimetre unit.
  2. Q₁ value = 8 + 0.75(12 − 8) = 11.00 cm.

questions.title: One extreme wait changes
questions.promptHtml:
The ordered waits are 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 minutes. The last wait is corrected from 9 to 29 minutes.

Find the new mean, median, range and IQR. Use quartile positions 0.25(n + 1) and 0.75(n + 1), with interpolation. Keep intermediate values unrounded.
questions.hint: Only the maximum changes. Check whether either quartile position uses that maximum.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The total rises from 44 to 64; mean = 64/8 = 8.00 minutes.
  2. The middle two values are still 5 and 6; median = 5.50 minutes.
  3. Range = 29 − 2 = 27.00 minutes.
  4. Q₁ at position 2.25 is 3.25; Q₃ at position 6.75 is 7.75. IQR = 4.50 minutes.
  5. Here the mean and range increase; the median and IQR remain unchanged.

questions.title: Can deleting an extreme value change the median?
questions.promptHtml:
The ordered observations are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 40. The observation 40 is excluded because it was outside the study period.

Calculate the original and revised medians, then assess the claim: “Deleting an extreme observation can never change the median.”
questions.hint: Deleting an observation changes the number of values and can change the middle position.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Original median = (3 + 4)/2 = 3.50.
  2. After deletion there are five observations; the median is the third value, 3.00.
  3. The claim is false. A median is resistant to extreme magnitudes, but it is not guaranteed to stay unchanged when observations are removed.

options.label: True: the median can never change
False: changing the number of observations can change the median

questions.title: CV is not a defect percentage
questions.promptHtml:
A sample of bottle fills has mean 250 mL and SD 5 mL. A trainee calculates CV = 2% and says: “Therefore, 2% of the bottles are defective.”

Which interpretation is correct?
questions.hint: CV compares SD with the mean. A defect rate needs an acceptance rule and counts of bottles outside that rule.
questions.solutionHtml: The SD is 2% of the mean fill. CV = 5/250 × 100 = 2%. This does not tell us the percentage of defective bottles; we need the permitted fill limits and relevant observations for that.

options.label: The SD is 2% of the mean fill
The next bottle has a 2% probability of being empty

questions.title: When is a CV comparison meaningful?
questions.promptHtml: You want to compare variation relative to the mean. Which situation is best suited to CV?
questions.hint: CV is most useful for positive ratio-scale measurements: zero represents absence of the measured quantity, and the mean is away from zero.
questions.solutionHtml: Positive bottle-fill volumes in mL have a meaningful zero and can support a relative-spread comparison. Celsius temperatures have an arbitrary zero; satisfaction codes are ordered categories; and division by a mean of zero is undefined.

options.label: Positive bottle-fill volumes in mL, with means well above zero
Signed changes whose mean is exactly zero

questions.title: Absolute and relative variation can disagree
questions.promptHtml:
Two positive output measures have these summaries: A: mean 10 units, SD 1 unit; B: mean 100 units, SD 5 units.

Calculate both CVs. Then identify the lower absolute SD and the lower relative variation.
questions.hint: Compare SDs for absolute variation. Compare SD/mean for relative variation.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. CV(A) = 1/10 × 100 = 10.00%.
  2. CV(B) = 5/100 × 100 = 5.00%.
  3. A has the lower absolute SD (1 versus 5 units), but B has the lower relative variation (5% versus 10%). The two comparisons answer different questions.

questions.title: Routine deliveries: average speed and consistency
questions.promptHtml:
A print shop tests two equally priced paper suppliers. Six trial delivery times, in hours, are:

A: 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, 60
B: 42, 44, 46, 48, 50, 52

These trials are samples used to estimate wider performance. Calculate each mean and sample SD (2 d.p.). For routine orders, the shop can order earlier and gives priority to lower variation in delivery time. Which supplier better meets this stated priority in the trial evidence?
questions.hint: Compare the average and spread separately. Use n − 1 = 5 for each sample variance.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Mean(A) = 270/6 = 45.00 hours; mean(B) = 282/6 = 47.00 hours.
  2. A: squared-deviation total 630; s = √(630/5) = 11.22 hours.
  3. B: squared-deviation total 70; s = √(70/5) = 3.74 hours.
  4. B better meets the priority of lower variation. It is two hours slower on average but has a much smaller sample SD. These small trials provide evidence, not a future guarantee.

extension.promptHtml: Optional written practice: give a two-sentence recommendation for routine orders, with numerical evidence and one limitation.
extension.modelAnswerHtml: I recommend B when lower variation is the priority: its sample SD is 3.74 hours compared with A’s 11.22 hours. B is slower on average (47 versus 45 hours), and six trials cannot guarantee future deliveries, so the shop should allow a time buffer.
rubric: States a recommendation linked to the given priority.
Compares both mean delivery times and both SDs with units.
Acknowledges the speed-versus-consistency trade-off.
States that a small set of trials does not guarantee future performance.

questions.title: An urgent order: the deadline changes the comparison
questions.promptHtml:
Six trial delivery times (hours) are A: 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, 60 and B: 42, 44, 46, 48, 50, 52.

questions.hint: Count times less than or equal to the deadline, divide by 6, and multiply by 100. Include a delivery exactly at the deadline.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. At 42 hours, A has 3/6 = 50.00% on time; B has 1/6 = 16.67%. A has the higher observed rate.
  2. At 54 hours, A has 5/6 = 83.33%; B has 6/6 = 100.00%. B has the higher observed rate.
  3. The comparison changes with the deadline. B’s six on-time trials at 54 hours do not guarantee the next delivery will be on time.

fields.label: Does B’s 100% trial rate guarantee the next arrival by 54 hours?

options.label: Yes: every future delivery is guaranteed

questions.title: Do not average group means equally
questions.promptHtml:
One ward treats 4 patients with mean wait 10 minutes. Another treats 12 patients with mean wait 18 minutes. A report says the combined mean is (10 + 18)/2 = 14 minutes.

Calculate the correct combined mean and identify the error.
questions.hint: Recover each total with count × mean. Then divide the combined total by the combined number of patients.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total wait = 4 × 10 + 12 × 18 = 40 + 216 = 256 minutes.
  2. Combined count = 16; combined mean = 256/16 = 16.00 minutes.
  3. The report gives equal weight to groups of different sizes. Each patient should have equal weight, not each ward.

questions.title: Work backwards from the mean and sample SD
questions.promptHtml:
Six observations have mean 10 and sample SD 2. Four values are 9, 10, 10 and 11; two are missing.

Find the smaller and larger missing values. Use both the mean and SD conditions.
questions.hint: The missing values sum to 20. The total squared deviation is (6 − 1) × 2² = 20; the known values contribute 2.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The total is 6 × 10 = 60. The known values sum to 40, so the missing values sum to 20.
  2. The total squared deviation is 5 × 4 = 20. The known squared deviations sum to 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 = 2, leaving 18.
  3. The missing deviations sum to zero, so write them as −d and +d. Then 2d² = 18, so d = 3.
  4. The missing values are 7 and 13. Their mean is 10 with the known values, and s = √(20/5) = 2.
